title: AI alignment
summary:
In the field of artificial intelligence (AI), alignment aims to steer AI systems toward a person's or group's intended goals, preferences, or ethical principles. An AI system is considered aligned if it advances the intended objectives, while a misaligned AI system pursues unintended objectives.

It is often difficult for AI designers to specify the full range of desired and undesired behaviors. Designers often use simpler proxy goals, such as gaining human approval, but proxy goals can overlook necessary constraints or reward the AI system for merely appearing aligned. AI systems may also find loopholes (reward hacking) to accomplish their proxy goals in unintended, sometimes harmful, ways. Advanced AI systems may develop unwanted instrumental strategies, such as seeking power or self-preservation, because such strategies help them achieve their assigned final goals.

The alignment problem has two parts. The first is the technical aspect, which focuses on how to formally encode values and principles into AI so that it does what it ought to do reliably. The second part is normative, which asks what moral values or principles we should encode in AI. Some researchers argue that it will be especially difficult to align advanced future AI systems, as more capable systems are better able to game their specifications, strategically mislead their designers, and protect and increase their power and intelligence.

A comprehensive survey on AI alignment identifies four key principles: Robustness, Interpretability, Controllability, and Ethicality (RICE). The landscape of alignment research is decomposed into forward alignment (making AI systems aligned via alignment training) and backward alignment (gaining evidence about alignment and governing systems appropriately to avoid misalignment risks). AI safety is a broader interdisciplinary field focused on preventing accidents, misuse, or other harmful consequences arising from AI systems, encompassing alignment, monitoring, and robustness.
